extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, law students, and legal academics seeking an overview of the Columbia Law Review
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the Columbia Law Review's identity, history, publication details, editorial governance, notable incidents, impact/rankings, and notable alumni. Useful as an encyclopedic overview rather than an author submission guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-edited journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Columbia Law Review is a law review edited and published by students at Columbia Law School.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates governance and editorial practice: student editors select, edit, and publish content. Relevant when evaluating the editorial model, contributor expectations, and how editorial decisions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content types published
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal publishes scholarly articles, essays, and student notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines acceptable submission types and the scope of work the Review disseminates. Authors should target scholarly articles, shorter essays, or student-authored notes aligned with legal scholarship norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets expectations for publication cadence and potential time-to-publication. Useful for assessing regularity and planning submissions or citation timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access status
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that published content is publicly accessible, which affects dissemination, copyright considerations, and author visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in Bluebook publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Columbia Law Review is one of four law reviews that publishes the Bluebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals institutional influence on citation norms and legal editorial standards. Relevant to citation style expectations and the Review's prominence in legal publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact and rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact factor (example): 2.224 (2018); among U.S. law journals as of 2025 ranked #1 by Washington and Lee University Law School and #4 by a University of Oregon professor (2023); top-cited law journal during the 2018 Supreme Court term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides bibliometric and reputation metrics used to evaluate journal influence and prestige. Includes specific ranking sources and historical citation performance; helpful for authors assessing journal standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexed in services such as JSTOR, Scopus, W&L; identifiers include CODEN (COLRAO), ISSN (0010-1958 print; 1945-2268 web), LCCN, OCLC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates discoverability and bibliographic metadata; relevant for librarians, authors, and evaluators tracking citations and archival access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical significance / longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of the current Columbia Law Review began in 1901, making it the fifth oldest surviving law review in the US.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaks to institutional legacy and prestige; can factor into perceptions of authority and tradition in legal scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial governance (board vs student editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review has a board of directors and student editors; the 2024 'Nakba' incident involved the board taking down the website and student editors voting to strike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights dual governance structure and potential for conflicts between directors and student editorial staff. Relevant for understanding decision-making authority, approval processes, and risks to editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial process transparency and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversy: the board stated the website was shut down due to the 'secretive' nature of the editorial process; student editors disputed that the editorial process was different from that used for all other articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises criteria for evaluating a journal's editorial transparency and independence (e.g., whether editorial decisions are consistent, whether processes are public or opaque). The Nakba episode serves as an example of how editorial opacity or perceived interference can affect staff actions and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website and publication control practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The board of directors took down the Review's website after publication of a controversial article, later restoring it and adding a statement; student editors published the article publicly as a free PDF when site was down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes practical control points (website hosting, content removal, public distribution) that can affect accessibility and crisis response. Relevant for contributors and stakeholders assessing where and how published content may be controlled or suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable alumni and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable alumni include U.S. Supreme Court Justices, federal judges, government officials, academic scholars, and prominent attorneys (e.g., Ruth Bader Ginsburg, William O. Douglas, Preet Bharara).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a proxy for the journal's influence on legal careers and networks; may inform perceptions of prestige and career impact for participants and contributors.
